0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

1.note: David is using this possessive form to mean salvation that would come to him or rescue that he would receive. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from saving me] or [from rescuing me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from saving me] or [from helping me]

David is using this possessive form to mean words that express his groaning or words spoken while groaning. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [far from my groaning words] or [far from the words I speak while groaning]

2.note: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I call to you by day, but you do not answer, and I call to you in the night]

By **there is no silence for me**, David means that he cannot rest or find peace because he is crying out to God throughout the night. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I cannot rest] or [and I find no peace]

3.note: Here the phrase **the praises of Israel** could (1) be using the word **praises** to represent the Tabernacle where the Israelite people offered God their praises. Alternate translation: [sitting in the praises of us Israelite people, that we give to you in your Tabernacle] or [sitting in your Tabernacle] (2) mean that Yahweh is the object of Israel’s praises. Alternate translation: [sitting as the object of the praises of Israel] or [ruling as the one whom Israel praises]

4.note: David is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our forefathers]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they trusted in you]

5.note: The expression **they were rescued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form, as in the UST, or in another way that is natural in your language.

6.note: Here David is speaking of himself as if he were a **worm**. He means that other people treat him as if he were worthless and do not care if he lives or not. If it would be helpful, you could use a comparable expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But I am treated as if I were a worthless worm and not a human]

By **a reproach of mankind**, David means that he has become someone whom all people mock and shame. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [someone whom people mock] or [an object of shame to everyone]

The expression **despised by the people** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the people despise me]

7.note: Here, **the lip** represents the mouth or speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they open their mouths wide] or [they sneer at me]

To **shake the head** was a symbolic action by which people showed contempt or mockery. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [They shake the head in mockery] or [They shake the head to show contempt]

8.q: גֹּ֣ל אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה יְפַלְּטֵ֑⁠הוּ יַ֝צִּילֵ֗⁠הוּ כִּ֘י חָ֥פֵֽץ בּֽ⁠וֹ
8.note: This is the beginning of what David’s enemies said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of these enemies. Alternate translation: [saying “Roll to Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him]

The enemies are using **Roll to** as a common expression of their culture to mean “commit your cause to” or “trust completely in.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Commit yourself to Yahweh] or [Trust completely in Yahweh]

In this verse, the first and third occurrence of the pronoun **him**, and the pronoun **he** refer to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [let Yahweh deliver him. Let Yahweh rescue him, since Yahweh delights in him]

The terms **deliver** and **rescue** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [let him save him]

9.note: The implication is that God was the one who brought David safely into the world at birth. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you are the one who brought me safely into the world]

By **making me trust upon the breasts of my mother**, David means that God caused him to trust in God even when he was a nursing infant dependent on his mother. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [causing me to trust in you while I nursed at my mother’s breasts]

10.note: Here David is speaking as if he were literally **cast** upon God. He means that he has been made to rely on God from the moment of his birth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have been caring for me from the womb] or [I have depended on you from birth]

The expression **I was cast** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [You took me as your own] or [Yahweh, you took care of me]

11.note: Here David is giving a command, **do not be far away from me**, but he intends it to communicate a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask you, please do not be far away from me] or [Yahweh, please do not be far away from me]

The implication is that David’s enemies or persecutors are approaching to harm him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for my enemies are approaching] or [for those who want to harm me are near]

12.q: סְ֭בָבוּ⁠נִי פָּרִ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים אַבִּירֵ֖י בָשָׁ֣ן כִּתְּרֽוּ⁠נִי
12.note: Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were **bulls** that **surround** and **encircle** him. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Many enemies surround me like bulls; strong ones like those of Bashan encircle me]

The phrase **strong ones of Bashan** gives further information about the **Many bulls**. (David refers to **Bashan** because it was known for its rich pasturelands and so the bulls there would have been well fed and strong.) David is not distinguishing these **strong ones** from other bulls that are not strong. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [the powerful bulls of Bashan] or [the mighty bulls of Bashan]

13.q: פָּצ֣וּ עָלַ֣⁠י פִּי⁠הֶ֑ם אַ֝רְיֵ֗ה טֹרֵ֥ף וְ⁠שֹׁאֵֽג
13.note: Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were **a tearing and roaring lion**. He means that they are fierce and dangerous and want to destroy him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They open their mouths against me, like a fierce, roaring lion that tears apart its prey]

14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **water** flows away and cannot be gathered back, so David feels completely drained of strength and energy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I am completely drained of strength like spilled water]

The expression **I am poured out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the same idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I pour out like water] or [I flow away like water]

David says **all of my bones are dislocated** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and my whole body is in pain] or [and I feel like my bones are coming apart]

14.q: הָיָ֣ה לִ֭בִּ⁠י כַּ⁠דּוֹנָ֑ג נָ֝מֵ֗ס בְּ⁠ת֣וֹךְ מֵעָֽ⁠י
14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **wax** melts and becomes soft when heated, so David’s **heart** has become weak and soft from fear and distress. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My heart has become weak like melted wax within me]

Here David is speaking of his **heart** as if it were **wax** that has melted. This image emphasizes how completely weak and helpless he feels in his distress. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My courage has completely failed me] or [I feel completely weak inside]

**Wax** is a soft, fatty substance that becomes liquid when heated and is used to make candles. If your readers would not be familiar with what wax is, you could use the name of a similar substance that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like soft fat] or [like something soft that melts]

15.note: David is making a comparison between his strength and **a shard**. The point of this comparison is that just as a shard is completely dried out and brittle, so is his strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My strength is completely dried up] or [I have lost my strength]

A **shard** was a piece of broken pottery. If your readers would not be familiar with what a shard is, in your translation you could use the name of a comparable object that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like a broken piece of pottery]

The expression **my tongue is being made to cling to my gums** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [my tongue clings to my gums] or [and you, Yahweh, allow me to suffer so that my tongue clings to my gums]

Here, **dust of death** represents the grave or dying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you lay me in the grave] or [and you bring me to death]

16.note: Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were **dogs** that hunt in packs. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [For my enemies have surrounded me like dogs]

The Hebrew text that the ULT is translated from reads **like the lion**. Other ancient manuscripts have a verb (instead of the noun translated as **like the lion**). At one point in the process of transmission, scribes may have mistakenly changed the last letter of the verb with the meaning “they have pierced” to a different (and similar looking) letter, resulting in the word **like the lion**. All the ancient versions of the Old Testament, as well as the early Jewish sources have verb forms instead of the noun form **like the lion**. The original text probably had the verb meaning “they have pierced” instead of the noun form translated **like the lion**. For this reason, you may wish to use the verb “they have pierced.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use whatever form it uses.

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [like the lion tears my hands and my feet] or [like the lion attacks my hands and my feet]

David is speaking of his enemies as if they were a **lion** tearing at his hands and feet. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [like a lion, they have mangled my hands and my feet]

17.note: David says **I can count all my bones** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [I am so thin and emaciated that I can count many of my bones] or [I am so thin and emaciated that people can see many of my bones]

The pronoun **They** refers to David’s enemies who have surrounded him (mentioned in the previous verses as “dogs” and “a company of ones doing evil”). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [My enemies look and they stare at me]
The implication is that David’s enemies stare at him and gloat. You could include this information, as in the UST, if that would be helpful to your readers.

19.note: David uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between his enemies who surround and torment him and Yahweh whom he calls upon for help. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, you] or [As for you]

19.q: וְ⁠אַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה אַל־תִּרְחָ֑ק אֱ֝יָלוּתִ֗⁠י לְ⁠עֶזְרָ֥תִ⁠י חֽוּשָׁ⁠ה
19.note: The phrases **do not be far away** and **hurry to help me** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than a commands. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [But you, Yahweh, please do not be far away. My strength, please hurry to help me]

The implication is that David wants Yahweh to come near to help him in his time of great distress. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [come near to help me] or [be close and help me]

David is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [be very near] or [stay close to me]

20.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please deliver]
Here, **sword** represents “death by violence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from death]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [deliver my only one from the hand of]

David is using **my only one** as a common expression of his culture to mean “my precious life” or “my dear life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my precious life]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of]

Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were **the dog**. This continues the imagery from verse 16 where enemies are described as dogs that have surrounded him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my enemies]

21.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please save me]

Here David is speaking as if his enemies were dangerous animals with **mouths** and **horns** that could attack and kill him. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [from my enemies who attack me like lions and wild oxen]

22.note: Here David is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will declare how wonderful you are] or [I will proclaim your character]

David is using the term **brothers** to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to my fellow Israelites]

23.q: כָּל־זֶ֣רַע יַעֲקֹ֣ב כַּבְּד֑וּ⁠הוּ וְ⁠ג֥וּרוּ מִ֝מֶּ֗⁠נּוּ כָּל־זֶ֥רַע יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
23.note: Here David is speaking of the descendants of Jacob, who Yahweh later renamed Israel, as if they were his **seed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the term “seed” in 18:50. Alternate translation: [All of the descendants of Jacob, honor him, and be terrified from him, all of you descendants of Israel]

24.note: David is using the adjective **afflicted** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the affliction of the afflicted person]

David is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [and he has shown his face to him] or [and he has listened to him]

David is using **hidden his face from him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “ignored him” or “refused to help him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he has not ignored him]

David assumes that readers will know that **he heard** means God heard his prayer and responded favorably to it. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he responded]

25.note: Here, **with you** represents “because of what you have done.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Because you have delivered me I praise you]

26.note: David is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [The poor ones] or [Poor people]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [will praise him]

David is using **May your heart live forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “May you live a long and prosperous life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you live long and prosper] or [May you have a long and blessed life]

The word **your** is plural here because David is addressing all the worshipers, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [your hearts]

27.note: Here the phrase, **the ends of the earth**, represents the people who live in the most distant places on earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [People everywhere on earth] or [People who live in the most distant places of the earth]

The implication is that the people **will remember** Yahweh and what he has done. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will remember Yahweh]

David is speaking as if people had been walking in one direction but then **turned** to walk toward Yahweh. He means that they will start worshiping and obeying Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and worship Yahweh] or [and start following Yahweh]

The implication is that all people groups or clans throughout the world will worship Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the people groups of the world]

To **bow down** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and submission. Sometimes it was also done as an act of worship. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation. Alternate translation: [and all the families of the nations will bow down in worship]
Here Yahweh’s **face** represents being in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your presence]

28.note: David assumes that readers will know that here the word **to** means “belongs” and that the word **kingdom** refers to Yahweh’s “reign.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For the kingship belongs to Yahweh] or [For Yahweh reigns as king]

29.q: אָכְל֬וּ וַ⁠יִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוּ֨וּ ׀ כָּֽל־דִּשְׁנֵי־אֶ֗רֶץ לְ⁠פָנָ֣י⁠ו יִ֭כְרְעוּ כָּל־יוֹרְדֵ֣י עָפָ֑ר
29.note: David is referring to all people by naming two extremes, **the fat of the earth** (the wealthy and prosperous who were well-fed and healthy), and **the ones going down to the dust** (the dying). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All people will eat and will bow down; to his face will kneel every person]
See how you translated this expression in 22:27.

David is using the adjective **fat** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the fat ones of the earth] or [the fat people of the earth]

Here, **the fat of the earth** represents the wealthy and prosperous people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the wealthy people of the earth] or [the prosperous people of the earth]
Here Yahweh’s **face** represents being in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in his presence]

To **kneel** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and submission to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [will kneel down in worship]

These two phrases **all of the ones going down to the dust** and **even his self he kept not alive** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [all of the ones going down to the dust, that is, those who cannot keep themselves alive]

Here the phrase **the ones going down to the dust** represents people who are dying or close to death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones going down to the grave] or [the ones who are dying]

The implication is that they were not able to keep themselves alive. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [even him who could not keep himself alive]

In this verse, the words **his** and **he** are singular in form, but they refer to all humans as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms of “his” and “he” or plural forms that include both men and women since this phrase refers to all people, as no one is able to keep themselves from eventually dying. Alternate translation: [even those who could not keep themselves alive]

30.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 22:23. Alternate translation: [Descendants will serve him]

The expression **it will be told** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will tell of the Lord to the next generation] or [people will tell the next generation about the Lord’s works]

David assumes that readers will know that **it** refers to the great works of the Lord that have been described throughout the psalm. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the next generation will be told about the great works of the lord]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to future generations] or [to the next generation]

31.q: וְ⁠יַגִּ֣ידוּ צִדְקָת֑⁠וֹ לְ⁠עַ֥ם נ֝וֹלָ֗ד כִּ֣י עָשָֽׂה
31.note: David is using the adjective **his righteousness** as a noun to mean something that shows God is righteous. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and will declare to a people who will be born, that because he is righteous, he has done it]

David assumes that readers will know **that he has done it** refers to God’s acts of deliverance and salvation described throughout the psalm. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [what he has done to save his people]
